problem: End-to-end ObjectNav policies keep their navigation history as an RNN recurrent state, which struggles to remember hundreds of low-level steps, or as a transformer episodic sequence, which ignores geometry and whose cost grows with episode length. Explicit semantic maps need heavy engineering, scale poorly to many object categories and are sensitive to sensor noise.
motivation: Efficient object search needs long-term, spatially organized scene memory, for example to backtrack or to exploit priors such as cushions being found in living rooms, without the hand design and precise localization that explicit SLAM maps require. The authors observe that episodic sequence memories carry large redundancy because navigation steps are small. A compact spatial latent grid that a learned module updates at every step could keep geometry awareness while staying end-to-end and cheap.
key_idea: Keep a small h×w grid of latent map tokens (a Recursive Implicit Map, RIM) that a transformer updates at every step together with the current observation token. The updated observation token predicts the action, and auxiliary tasks (visual-feature prediction at a queried pose, explicit occupancy-map reconstruction, semantic prediction) push the map toward encoding geometry and semantics.
insight: Recursive transformer updating is the main source of the gain, not memory size. Table II shows a 1×1 implicit map (45.74 SR) already beats an LSTM-style recurrent state with the same memory size (Table I, 38.95 SR) and an episodic sequence with T×d memory (Table I, 44.51 SR), showing that per-step sequence memory is redundant. Map size helps up to 5×5 (49.52 SR) and saturates at 7×7, which the authors link to MP3D's roughly 8 m average start-to-goal distance. The auxiliary tasks are complementary (Table III): visual-feature prediction gives about 11% relative SPL/SoftSPL gain (15.12→16.86 SPL), semantic prediction mainly raises SR, and all three together give the best SR, 50.25 (Table III, last row). Dropping the agent pose only reduces SR from 47.74 to 47.43, so the map can be updated from visual features alone; this robustness is what allows pose-free real-robot deployment.
method: Observation encoding: frozen CLIP ResNet50 encodes RGB and a frozen PointNav-pretrained ResNet50 encodes depth. Pose (x, y, sinθ, cosθ) relative to the start goes through its own linear layer, and the previous action and goal category use lookup embeddings. Linear hidden sizes are 128/256/64/32/32. Features are concatenated and a sinusoidal step embedding is added to form token o_t.

Recursive implicit map: M^t is an h×w grid (default 3×3) of d=512 latent cells. It is initialized as a learnable embedding plus an FFN of the cell offset (i−h/2, j−w/2). At each step a 4-layer transformer self-attends over [map cells; o_t], with map-cell and agent position features added inside the attention softmax. The output map tokens become M^{t+1}.
Action prediction: the updated observation token ô_t goes through a single-layer FFN and softmax over 6 discrete actions. Training is behavior cloning with inflection-weighted cross-entropy (γ=3.48).

Auxiliary visual feature prediction: a query-pose token for a random pose at t'∈[0, t+k], with k=20 so it can include near-future poses, attends to the map through an attention mask so it never influences the map update. It predicts the CLIP feature at that pose, trained with a contrastive loss using cosine similarity against other trajectory features.
Auxiliary explicit mapping: an FFN decodes M^t into a 48×48 egocentric 2-channel map (occupied / explored, 25 cm cells), trained with BCE against maps built from ground-truth depth and pose.

Auxiliary semantic prediction: predicts per-category object existence and mask-area ratio from the RGB-D features, using BCE with simulator labels. The total loss is L = L_AP + 0.3·(L_VP + L_EM + L_SP).

Inference and deployment: take the argmax action and, in simulation, switch to the second-best action on a detected collision. On the real robot, a lidar check replaces forward moves near obstacles, the pose input is dropped, and the camera is tilted −20°. An optional ViT-Adapter ADE20K segmentation plus depth provides a stop trigger (median target distance <1 m and area >1%).

setting.backbone: Frozen CLIP ResNet50 (RGB) + frozen PointNav-pretrained ResNet50 (depth) + 4-layer transformer (hidden 512) map updater/policy trained from scratch with behavior cloning
setting.training_data: Habitat-web human demonstrations: 70k ObjectNav trajectories in 56 MP3D training scenes (21 categories), with simulator semantic labels and GT depth/pose maps for the auxiliary losses. For the real robot: retrained on demos re-rendered with a virtual 120 cm, 55°×42° camera, then fine-tuned on 20/35/70 real teleoperated Tiago++ demonstrations (120 iterations).
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + agent pose relative to start (GPS/compass-like) + previous action + goal category; pose dropped for the real-robot model
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOK_UP/DOWN 30°, STOP; 500-step budget
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT semantics/maps used only as training labels); in simulation the agent pose is used to detect collisions and pick the second-best action

numbers_note: Real-robot results (Tiago++, 7 categories, 10 episodes each) are reported only as per-category success counts in Table VII and are not listed above. Examples: 35 demos without segmentation gives Chair 10/10, Cushion 3/10, Plant 5/10, Table 7/10, Sink 6/10, Sofa 8/10, Toilet 4/10; 70 demos underperforms 35. Other ablations are omitted: map size 1×1/5×5/7×7 gives 45.74/49.52/48.52 SR, and the other auxiliary-task combinations are in Table III.
results: On MP3D val, RIM reaches 50.3 SR / 17.0 SPL, clearly beating the strongest implicit baseline Habitat-web (35.4 / 10.2) and the explicit-map STUBBORN (37.0 SR). On the MP3D test-standard split it reaches 37.6 / 15.6 against Habitat-web's 27.8 / 9.9 and ranked 1st on the leaderboard. Trained only on MP3D, it transfers to HM3D with 57.8 / 27.2 on val (MP3D-trained SemExp: 50.8 / 21.7) and 61.4 / 29.3 on test-standard, competitive with HM3D-trained OVRL (60.0 / 27.0). Against matched memory baselines, it beats an episodic transformer sequence (44.51 SR) and a recurrent state (38.95 SR) and runs 1.36× faster than the former. On a real Tiago++ robot, fine-tuning on only 20–70 real demos gives encouraging per-category success.
limitations: The sim-to-real gap is large: the robot is bigger than the simulated agent and collides on edges, discrete 30°/0.25 m actions make narrow passages such as restroom doors hard, and incomplete MP3D meshes give observations with holes that do not match real images.

The auxiliary tasks need privileged simulator labels at training time (semantic annotations, GT depth/pose-based maps), and training relies on 70k human demonstrations. Fine-tuning on more real demos (70) generalized worse than 35.

There is a large val–test gap on MP3D (50.3 vs 37.6 SR), which the authors attribute to long-tailed category distributions. The map size saturates at 7×7, suggesting limited capacity for larger environments.
